data.raw_text:
🚨Why We’re Eating the Future to Pay the Past

Imagine buying a full sack of rice for your family, but before you get home, an invisible hand reaches inside and takes a large portion away. You paid the full price, yet your family receives less food than they should.

You paid for the full bag. But you never truly owned it.
That ghost is the ₱18.49 trillion debt of the Philippines.

Right now, the country feels like a father working endless double shifts while the bank takes most of his salary before he even touches it. We are no longer simply borrowing money. We are sacrificing the future of our children just to keep the machine alive.

🚨The Fire Called Interest

Every single day, the Philippine government spends around ₱1.8 billion on interest payments alone.

Not the debt itself.

Just the price of remaining buried in debt.

Every 24 hours, that amount could have built:

➡️3,600 new classrooms

➡️12,000 public hospital beds

➡️4 million meals for hungry children

Instead, the money disappears into the furnace of interest payments.

We celebrate massive infrastructure projects as symbols of progress, yet many are quietly paid for by the medicine our grandparents will never receive and the education our children will never fully have.
The Parasite in the System
Debt behaves like a parasite.
It always feeds on the weakest first.

Politicians rarely feel the pain. Ordinary Filipinos do.

It is the exhausted mother waiting ten hours in a crowded public clinic because there are not enough doctors.

It is the student sweating inside an overcrowded classroom while using books older than they are.

We are trying to build a golden age on unstable ground. Every shiny bridge and towering project risks becoming another chain tied around the neck of future generations.

🚨The Brutal Truth

We have become a nation trapped in a cycle of borrowing.

We borrow to pay old debt.
Then we borrow again to fund new projects.
Then we borrow once more just to pay the interest on previous loans.

If this continues, the Philippines risks becoming more than a struggling nation. It risks becoming a collection of assets slowly controlled by foreign creditors and financial institutions.

Right now, the system appears stable only because the final bill has not yet arrived.

But someday it will.

And when that day comes, it will not be today’s leaders who carry the burden.

It will be our children. The future is no longer being prepared. It is already being sold.
